questions.text: A partnership of four architects has one non-architect investor who owns 30 percent. What action must the partnership take?

options.text: No action is required; the partnership is compliant under current regulations.
The partnership must immediately register with the SEC to ensure legal compliance.
The partnership must adjust ownership to achieve 75 percent RLA composition
The non-architect must obtain an architecture license to maintain the partnership's legal standing.

rationale.a: Falsely assumes compliance—70% architect ownership falls short of the 75% threshold; the partnership violates RA 9266.
rationale.b: Repeats existing step without fixing the problem—registration status is not the issue; ownership composition violates the law.
rationale.d: Presents impossible solution—non-architect investors cannot obtain architecture licenses by definition; only architects can be licensed.
rationale.correct: With one non-architect owning 30 percent, architects own only 70 percent, violating the 75 percent RLA requirement. The partnership must adjust ownership or re-register to comply.
rationale.takeaway: A non-architect investor's 30% stake reduces architect ownership to 70%, violating the 75% RLA requirement and forcing ownership restructure.

questions.text: What is the relationship between a partnership agreement and the liability of individual partners?

options.text: The partnership agreement eliminates all personal liability, which is a common misconception
The partnership agreement can limit liability among partners through indemnity clauses
Joint and several liability cannot be modified by agreement, ensuring partners remain accountable
The agreement must be approved by the PRC before liability effects apply, which is a regulatory requirement

rationale.a: Overstates agreement power—agreements cannot eliminate statutory joint and several liability to third-party clients.
rationale.c: Understates agreement power—while statutory liability to clients cannot be modified, inter-partner apportionment through indemnity is permitted.
rationale.d: Imposes false requirement—partnership agreements do not require PRC approval for internal liability allocation mechanisms.
rationale.correct: While joint and several liability exists by law, partnership agreements can include indemnification clauses to apportion liability among partners or protect one partner from another's malpractice.
rationale.takeaway: Partnership agreements cannot eliminate joint and several liability to clients, but indemnity clauses redistribute liability among partners internally.

questions.text: A three-partner architectural firm loses one partner who retires. One remaining partner becomes incapacitated. Can the surviving partner continue the practice legally?

options.text: No, the partnership dissolves; the surviving architect must register as sole proprietorship with DTI and PRC
No, the partnership must be dissolved immediately, and all ongoing projects must be reassigned to a new legal entity
Only if a new partner is added before the incapacitated partner leaves, ensuring continuity of the firm's legal status
Only with prior approval from the PRC, which must be obtained through a formal application process

rationale.b: Imposes automatic dissolution incorrectly—partners can continue if the agreement permits and RLA requirements are met.
rationale.c: Sets unnecessary precondition—timing of new partner addition is irrelevant; current composition after withdrawal is what matters.
rationale.d: Imposes false requirement—PRC approval is not needed for continuation; partnership agreement and RLA composition determine legality.
rationale.correct: Continuation after partner withdrawal depends on the partnership agreement and whether remaining architects meet the 75 percent RLA requirement; re-registration may be required.
rationale.takeaway: Partnership cannot continue with one architect; must dissolve and surviving architect register as sole proprietorship.

questions.text: When a partner withdraws from an architectural partnership, what must happen regarding projects in progress?

options.text: All projects must be terminated immediately, regardless of their stage of completion, to prevent liability issues
Outstanding projects and architect-of-record status must be transferred
The withdrawn partner retains liability for incomplete projects, unless otherwise agreed in the partnership contract
The BOA automatically assumes project responsibility, ensuring continuity of service without interruption

rationale.a: Creates unnecessary disruption—projects can be transferred to continuing partners; immediate termination is not required.
rationale.c: Perpetuates liability incorrectly—withdrawn partners cannot indefinitely bear liability; transfer of architect-of-record extinguishes their responsibility.
rationale.d: Attributes false authority—BOA does not assume operational responsibility for specific projects; only licensed architects can be architect-of-record.
rationale.correct: When a partner withdraws, outstanding client relationships and project obligations must be transferred to a continuing partner or assigned to another licensed architect with client notification.
rationale.takeaway: Partner withdrawal requires transferring architect-of-record status and client projects to continuing partners or other RLAs with client notification.

questions.text: What must a partnership agreement establish regarding architectural document ownership after dissolution?

options.text: All documents revert to the PRC, ensuring that regulatory oversight is maintained even after the partnership ends
Documents are distributed equally among former partners, unless otherwise specified in a pre-existing agreement or clause
Ownership transfer procedures and assignment mechanisms must be specified
Documents automatically become public property, accessible to anyone who requests them under the Freedom of Information Act

rationale.a: Attributes false ownership to regulatory body—PRC does not own practitioner documents; the partnership or its successors retain ownership.
rationale.b: Imposes equal distribution—equal distribution may not reflect each partner's contribution; the agreement should specify actual allocation.
rationale.d: Converts private property to public incorrectly—architectural documents remain proprietary; dissolution does not make them public.
rationale.correct: Partnership agreements must address intellectual property ownership and transfer procedures for architectural documents to prevent disputes after partner withdrawal or partnership dissolution.
rationale.takeaway: Partnership agreements must specify how architectural documents are assigned after dissolution to prevent disputes over intellectual property.

questions.text: What percentage of partnership ownership must be held by registered and licensed architects?

options.text: 51 percent minimum
60 percent minimum
75 percent minimum
100 percent required

rationale.a: Mistakes the 51% simple majority rule for general corporations with the 75% RLA requirement specific to architectural firms.
rationale.b: Underestimates the actual requirement—60% falls short of the 75% threshold needed to ensure professional control.
rationale.d: Overreaches by requiring 100%—the law allows up to 25% non-architect participation while maintaining professional control.
rationale.correct: RA 9266 Section 37 mandates that registered and licensed architects compose at least 75 percent of owners and decision-makers to prevent non-architect control of architectural firms.
rationale.takeaway: The 75% RLA rule applies equally to partnerships and corporations—architects must control at least three-quarters of ownership.

questions.text: Which government agencies must approve an architectural partnership under RA 9266?

options.text: SEC and DTI
BOA and PRC only
SEC and BOA
PRC and Department of Finance

rationale.a: Confuses partnership registration with sole proprietorship—DTI registers sole proprietors, not partnerships; SEC registers partnerships.
rationale.b: Omits the required SEC registration—partnerships cannot skip corporate registration with SEC; BOA and PRC registration alone is insufficient.
rationale.d: Substitutes Finance Department for SEC—only SEC registers partnerships; Department of Finance has no partnership registration authority.
rationale.correct: Architectural partnerships must be registered first with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), then with the Board of Architecture (BOA), subject to PRC approval, for registration certificate.
rationale.takeaway: Partnerships register with SEC for corporate formation, then BOA for architectural practice approval.

questions.text: In an architectural partnership, who bears liability for one partner's professional negligence?

options.text: Only the negligent partner personally, as they are solely responsible for their professional actions and decisions.
Only the partnership entity, which assumes all legal and financial responsibilities for the actions of its partners.
All partners jointly and severally
The BOA and PRC, as they oversee professional conduct and enforce disciplinary measures.

rationale.a: Mistakes sole proprietorship liability for partnership—partnerships spread liability to all partners, not confined to the negligent one.
rationale.b: Misunderstands joint and several liability—the partnership entity is liable but so are individual partners personally.
rationale.d: Attributes liability to regulatory bodies—BOA and PRC enforce standards but do not bear civil liability for architect negligence.
rationale.correct: Partners share joint and several liability; each partner is personally liable for acts and omissions of other partners within the scope of partnership business, exposing all partners' personal assets.
rationale.takeaway: In partnerships, one partner's negligence creates liability for all partners' personal assets—joint and several liability means clients can sue anyone.

questions.text: What is the primary purpose of the 75 percent RLA majority rule in partnerships?

options.text: To increase government tax collection, ensuring that partnerships contribute fairly to public revenue
To ensure professional standards are maintained by architects
To limit the number of partnerships allowed, preventing market saturation
To prevent competition from corporations, safeguarding the interests of individual practitioners

rationale.a: Confuses regulatory purpose with revenue—the rule addresses professional control, not tax benefits.
rationale.c: Mistakes the rule as quantitative cap—the rule ensures quality control, not supply control.
rationale.d: Misrepresents inter-structural competition—the rule applies uniformly to partnerships and corporations alike.
rationale.correct: The RLA majority rule prevents non-architects from directing professional decisions and ensures that architectural standards and ethics are maintained by qualified architects.
rationale.takeaway: The 75% RLA rule protects professional integrity by ensuring architects control decisions, not financial investors.

questions.text: What is the minimum number of partners required to form an architectural partnership?

options.text: One architect
Two or more architects
Three architects minimum
Five or more architects

rationale.a: Confuses sole proprietorship with partnership—one architect forms a sole proprietorship, not a partnership.
rationale.c: Sets an unnecessarily high threshold—partnerships form with two architects minimum, not three.
rationale.d: Creates an unrealistically high barrier—while partnerships can have five members, they do not require this minimum.
rationale.correct: An architectural partnership requires at least two registered/licensed architects composing 75% ownership per RA 9266 Sec 37, formed among architects or with allied professionals and registered with SEC and BOA.
rationale.takeaway: Partnership minimally requires two RLAs; one architect alone is a sole proprietorship, not a partnership.
